card.keepWhy: However long you’ve been gone, there’s light waiting.
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Rama, Sita and Lakshmana return to Ayodhya after fourteen years and the war; Ayodhya celebrates; Rama is crowned)
North Indian Diwali tradition: Ayodhya lit lamps for Rama’s return on the new-moon night of Kartika
The film’s note: elsewhere Diwali honors Lakshmi, or Krishna’s victory over Narakasura
check: The new-moon night and the lamps lit for Rama’s return are festival tradition, not details in Valmiki (where Ayodhya greets him with decorated streets); the film tells them as story before “that’s how many Hindus in North India explain Diwali.” Confirm.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever come back after being away a long time? to a city, a family, your faith, yourself.
options: then you know this feeling. listen.
then this one is for you. listen.
good. keep this light for later.

steps.line: After fourteen years in exile, after the war, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana finally headed home to Ayodhya.

steps.q: While Rama was away those fourteen years, who ruled Ayodhya?
o: Queen Kaikeyi, who sent him away
Bharata, with Rama’s sandals on the throne
King Dasharatha, waiting for his son
steps.why: His brother Bharata refused the crown and ruled in Rama’s name, with Rama’s sandals on the throne. King Dasharatha had died of grief soon after Rama left.

steps.line: It was a dark, new-moon night. No moon at all.

steps.q: It’s a new-moon night, pitch dark. How do you think the city lights their way?
o: The palace lights the main road
Every home lights its own lamps
steps.why: Not one big light from the palace: every household lit its own. That’s still Diwali, each home setting out its own row of lamps.

steps.line: So the people lit lamps. One, then another, then thousands.
Along every street and every rooftop, so they could find their way home.

steps.q: Diwali falls on the new moon of Kartika, the darkest night of the month. Why would the story need that night?
o: So the lamps have the most dark to beat
Because travel was safer without a moon
Because the new moon is lucky for kings
steps.why: Many Hindus read Diwali as light beating darkness, so the festival sits on a moonless night, when every lamp counts most.

steps.line: That’s how many Hindus in North India explain Diwali: the whole city lit up, to say welcome back.
steps.label: Diwali

steps.q: In much of South India, Diwali tells a different victory. Whose?
steps.why: In Tamil Nadu and much of the South, Diwali morning marks Krishna’s defeat of Narakasura. In Bengal the same night is Kali Puja. Many stories, one row of lamps.

steps.line: No matter how long you’ve been gone, there’s light waiting for you.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Match each Diwali custom to what it says.
pairs: a welcome for whoever’s coming home
steps.why: Many families clean top to bottom before Diwali, because Lakshmi, goddess of fortune, is said to visit homes that are clean and bright.

say: here’s what i love. nobody asked rama where he’d been. they just lit the way home.
for many hindus, diwali says light wins over darkness, and there’s always a way back. no matter how long you’ve been gone, a lamp is waiting.

steps.q: Diwali comes from Deepavali: deepa means lamp, and avali means row. After this story, why is that the perfect name?
o: Lamps in every row of Rama’s army
Rows of lamps lit the road home
The rows of people who lined the streets
steps.why: Deepavali: a row of lamps. The festival’s name is the welcome itself.

today.say: tonight, light a candle or a lamp for someone, or something, you want to welcome back. maybe a friend, maybe a part of yourself. many hindus light a diya with a short prayer. you can say one, or just light it. it’s your choice.
options: then light it tonight. that’s a homecoming.
then welcome yourself back. you’re allowed.
